scenario.name: Microsoft MSRC & CISA KEV DFIR — ASP.NET / SharePoint __VIEWSTATE MachineKey LosFormatter Deserialization Forensics
scenario.overview: Picture a cozy corner coffee shop and co-working cafe with a striped storefront awning, warm wooden espresso bar, glass pastry case, and laptops open across bistro tables. Sitting quietly at a corner bistro table near the espresso bar, a patron sets up a lookalike free coffee-shop guest board to attract nearby customers. In this real-world scenario, the intruder quietly copies a trusted access pass from the cafe barista's station, then quietly copies a trusted access pass from the cafe barista's station. The cafe manager notices a strange second sign-in notice taped beside the pastry case and alerts customers to the fake hotspot at the corner table. In this scenario (T1190, Microsoft MSRC & CISA KEV DFIR, ASP.NET / SharePoint __VIEWSTATE MachineKey LosFormatter Deserialization Forensics), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: web.config <machineKey> validationKey, then signed __VIEWSTATE LosFormatter /, then w3wp.exe Child Process Creation. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering web.config <machineKey> validationKey, then Signed __VIEWSTATE LosFormatter /, then w3wp.exe Child Process Creation, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 2: Signed __VIEWSTATE LosFormatter / TypeConfuseDelegate Deserialization (IIS W3C Access Log)
stages.subtitle: Execution (T1059 - Signed LosFormatter .NET Gadget Deserialization)
stages.description: As regulars order lattes from the barista and type in their work details at the window tables, their conversations and login slips pass straight across the eavesdropper’s table. Here in Step 2 inside the coffee shop, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the cafe order register in tiny disguised batches without disturbing the roastery bean storage room. Once the attacker obtains the web.config validationKey (via a path traversal, backup leak, or CVE-2023-29357 auth bypass), they sign a TypeConfuseDelegate / ActivitySurrogateSelector gadget chain with HMACSHA256 and submit it via POST /_layouts/15/Picker.aspx (or GET ?__VIEWSTATE=/wEPDwUK...). Because the HMAC is valid, HTTP 200 is returned in the IIS W3C log (C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\W3SVC1\u_ex*.log) with an abnormally large cs-bytes (request size) or cs-uri-query (logged in Network Event 200 with LogFile=C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\W3SVC1\u_ex261103.log, UriStem=/_layouts/15/Picker.aspx, RequestBytes=cs-bytes=8420 , Signed ObjectStateFormatter Payload, HttpStatus=200 OK , HMAC Validation Passed so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact).
